guidance.when: The agreement addresses reverse engineering of confidential, proprietary, embodied, or disclosed information.
guidance.inspection: An operative prohibition on the receiving party reverse engineering the protected information, including having another person do so, establishes the hypothesis. A prior-written-consent qualification does not erase the prohibition. Restrictions on copying, analysis, independent development, or general misuse are insufficient without reverse-engineering language.
guidance.evidence_requirement: Cite the operative reverse-engineering prohibition and any qualifier defining the protected material or permitted consent route.

operations.rationale: Case 613 supplies a direct, successful witness for a narrow reusable rule; the new procedure distinguishes express reverse-engineering restrictions from merely related use or copying provisions.

guidance.when: Assessing whether the receiving party may make a copy in some circumstance.
guidance.inspection: Require an affirmative operational copying route. This includes an express exception allowing copies as necessary for an authorized evaluation, permitted disclosure, performance of obligations, exercise of contractual rights, or accomplishment of the stated purpose. Prepared analyses or compilations do not alone authorize copying. A prohibition qualified only by prior consent or approval, or a remedy for unauthorized copying, is not an existing operational permission.
guidance.evidence_requirement: Cite the copying clause and the language defining the authorized circumstance; include a governing introduction when the permission is expressed as an exception to a prohibition.

operations.rationale: The revision separates operational exceptions that themselves authorize necessary copying (261, 487, 622, 613) from a mere prior-approval qualifier, which did not establish permission in 159.

guidance.when: The agreement prohibits copying confidential information.
guidance.inspection: A direct copy ban establishes contradiction only when the complete agreement provides no operational copying route. An exception for copies necessary for permitted disclosure, evaluation, performance, exercising contractual rights, or the stated purpose is an affirmative route and defeats this condition. A prior-consent or prior-approval qualifier alone is not such a route.
guidance.evidence_requirement: Cite the copy prohibition and inspect the complete agreement for operational exceptions or backup permissions; do not call the ban unqualified when its own exception authorizes necessary copying.

operations.rationale: Different-label witnesses show the separating condition: operational necessity exceptions support permission, while consent-only bans and bans lacking a copying exception support contradiction.

guidance.when: The agreement expressly prohibits disclosure to third parties while identifying limited permitted recipients.
guidance.inspection: Establish contradiction only from a direct prohibition using third-party language when the complete agreement supplies no permission for consultants, agents, advisers, affiliates, contractors, or other non-employees. An internal-staff or employee permission, combined only with a general confidentiality duty, is not enough to infer the benchmark contradiction. A consent possibility alone is not an existing sharing permission.
guidance.evidence_requirement: Cite the express third-party prohibition and inspect all disclosure exceptions for an independent non-employee route. Do not rely solely on an employee-only exception or general nondisclosure language.

operations.rationale: Case 430 supports contradiction from an express third-party ban, whereas 377 and 159 show that internal or employee access plus general confidentiality should not be expanded into that result; 92 confirms that an adviser or consultant exception defeats it.

guidance.when: The agreement requires return or destruction of confidential information and copies without stating a retention exception.
guidance.inspection: Confirm that the command reaches all confidential information in the relevant possession or control and all copies, and that no retained subset is authorized. A duty limited to documents, tangible items, records, or deliverable material is not exhaustive merely because it covers all items within that narrower category. Survival of confidentiality or non-use duties is not a return command.
guidance.evidence_requirement: Cite the complete operative duty establishing coverage of all confidential information and copies, and verify across the agreement that no backup, archival, legal-copy, or other retention exception applies.

operations.rationale: Contradiction witnesses 416, 487, 159, and 92 use comprehensive information-and-copies duties; 377 and 290 show that narrower tangible-document or record duties must not be treated as exhaustive.

guidance.when: The definition or coverage clause addresses communication form.
guidance.inspection: Require explicit form language linking oral or verbal disclosures to protected information, including coverage regardless of form or whether reduced to writing. References to discussions, negotiations, meetings, business information, or information that happens to be communicable orally do not establish oral coverage. Derivative notes or documents are also insufficient.
guidance.evidence_requirement: Cite the definition or coverage language expressly mentioning oral, verbal, form-independent, or not-reduced-to-writing communication, with any continuation needed to connect it to confidential information.

operations.rationale: Successful witnesses expressly address oral, verbal, or form-independent disclosure, while 273, 377, and 430 demonstrate that discussions, meetings, or non-technical subject matter cannot substitute for communication-form language.

guidance.when: The agreement addresses ownership, licenses, or rights in confidential information or associated intellectual property.
guidance.inspection: Look for an express statement that disclosure or the agreement grants, conveys, confers, or implies no license or right. An authorization to use information, even broadly or with consent, does not by itself contradict a no-license proposition. But a residual-information use right paired only with a disclaimer of patent, copyright, or trademark licensing does not establish that no rights are granted in confidential information generally.
guidance.evidence_requirement: Cite the express no-grant clause and its object. Use an ownership clause only when it connects the denied right to confidential information; do not infer the result solely from a use restriction, consent route, or residuals clause.

operations.rationale: The update preserves express no-grant successes while separating them from broad-use or consent provisions and from the mixed residuals clause in 622, which expressly denied only specified intellectual-property licenses.

guidance.when: The agreement addresses information obtained from an external source or later made available non-confidentially.
guidance.inspection: Require that information actually becomes available to or is received or learned by the receiving party from a source other than the disclosing party or its representatives, with that source free of confidentiality restrictions. A statement that information is already known to unspecified others, a generic exception introduction, public availability alone, or independent development does not establish third-party acquisition. Information routed through the disclosing party remains within the protected channel.
guidance.evidence_requirement: Cite the external-source receipt item and its governing exclusion introduction, including the condition on the source's authority or confidentiality duty; never cite the introduction alone.

operations.rationale: Positive witnesses contain an actual external-source receipt route; 430, 613, and 383 show that information known to others, an exception preamble alone, or unrelated authorization cannot substitute for that route.
